practice_questions.text: Identify one inherited condition that can affect an individual's health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for one correct identification:
• Sickle cell disease (1)
• Cystic fibrosis (1).

practice_questions.text: Give two physical effects that a person with cystic fibrosis may experience.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each correct physical effect (max 2):
• Thick mucus builds up in the lungs (1)
• Frequent chest infections (1)
• Difficulty breathing (1)
• Problems absorbing nutrients from food (1)
• Need for daily physiotherapy (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how obesity can have a negative effect on an individual's emotional and social wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for developed explanation across emotional and social wellbeing:
• Obesity can cause low self-esteem (1) because the individual may feel unhappy with their appearance or physical abilities (1).
• Obesity can lead to social isolation (1) because the individual may experience bullying or discrimination from others, causing them to withdraw from social activities (1).
• Accept other valid chains linking obesity to emotional or social effects.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how mental ill health, such as anxiety, can affect an individual's health and wellbeing across all areas of PIES.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed discussion covering multiple PIES areas with developed points.
Mid band (3-4): Some discussion with partial development.
Lower band (1-2): Limited points with little development.
Indicative content:
• Physical: racing heart, sweating, difficulty sleeping, weakened immune system
• Intellectual: difficulty concentrating, poor performance at school or work
• Emotional: persistent worry, low self-esteem, feeling unable to cope
• Social: avoiding social situations, withdrawing from friends and family, difficulty maintaining relationships
• Links between areas, e.g. poor sleep (physical) leading to difficulty concentrating (intellectual).

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which inherited conditions have a greater impact on an individual's health and wellbeing than physical ill health conditions such as obesity or type 2 diabetes.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive evaluation with balanced argument and justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good evaluation with some balance.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some evaluation with limited balance.
Lower band (1-2): Limited evaluation.
Indicative content:
Inherited conditions:
• Present from birth — individual has no control
• Often lifelong with no cure (e.g. sickle cell, cystic fibrosis)
• Affect PIES from an early age — missed education, social isolation from childhood
• Daily treatment regimes can be exhausting and restrictive
Physical ill health:
• Often linked to lifestyle choices — some can be prevented or managed
• Obesity and type 2 diabetes can be improved with diet and exercise
• However, CVD can be fatal if not managed
• Social stigma around obesity can severely affect emotional wellbeing
Conclusion: Both have significant impacts but inherited conditions may be considered greater because the individual has no control and they are lifelong. However, the impact depends on the severity of the condition, the support available, and the individual's circumstances.

practice_questions.text: Amir is 45 years old. He was recently diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure. He works long hours in a stressful office job and rarely exercises. He has also been feeling anxious about his health. Using the case study, assess how Amir's physical factors are affecting his overall health and wellbeing. In your answer, consider the impact on his physical, intellectual, emotional, and social wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (8-10): Comprehensive, well-developed response covering all PIES areas with clear links to Amir's specific circumstances. Chains of reasoning throughout.
Upper-mid band (5-7): Good coverage of multiple PIES areas with some developed links to the case study.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points but limited development or links to Amir.
Lower band (1-2): Basic points with little reference to the case study.
Indicative content:
• Physical: Type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure increase risk of CVD, stroke, kidney damage. Lack of exercise worsens both conditions. Fatigue and physical symptoms reduce his ability to function.
• Intellectual: Stress and anxiety can cause difficulty concentrating at work. High blood sugar levels can cause brain fog. This may affect his job performance.
• Emotional: Anxiety about his health creates persistent worry. He may feel guilty about his lifestyle. Low mood and fear about long-term complications. Stress from work compounds his emotional state.
• Social: Long working hours reduce time for socialising. Anxiety may cause him to withdraw from friends and family. He may avoid social events involving food or alcohol due to his diabetes.
• Links between factors: stress (mental ill health) raises blood pressure (physical ill health), creating a negative cycle. Lack of exercise worsens both diabetes and anxiety.
• Person-specific: At 45, Amir is in middle adulthood where health risks increase naturally. His stressful job is both a cause and an aggravating factor.

practice_questions.text: Identify one type of barrier that could prevent an individual from accessing a health service.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark(s) for any one of: physical barrier (1), sensory disability barrier (1), social/cultural barrier (1), language/speech barrier (1), geographical barrier (1), resource barrier (1), financial barrier (1).

practice_questions.text: Give two personal obstacles that could make it difficult for an individual to follow health recommendations.
practice_questions.marks: 1 marks for each obstacle, up to 2 marks: emotional/psychological factors such as low motivation or low self-esteem (1), time constraints due to work/family commitments (1), availability of resources/financial constraints (1), unachievable targets (1), lack of support from family/friends (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a barrier and an obstacle in health and social care.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks: a barrier is something unique to the health and social care system that prevents access (1), an obstacle is something personal to the individual that blocks them from moving forward (1), example of a barrier e.g. no wheelchair ramp at a clinic (1), example of an obstacle e.g. low self-esteem making someone reluctant to attend (1).

practice_questions.text: Sonia is 70 and speaks Polish as her first language. She has been advised to attend a diabetes management class at the local hospital, which is 12 miles away. Discuss the barriers Sonia may face when trying to follow this recommendation.
practice_questions.marks: Indicative content: Language barrier — class may be delivered in English, information leaflets may not be in Polish (1). Geographical barrier — hospital 12 miles away, may have poor transport links (1). Ways to overcome — interpreter service (1), literature in Polish (1), community transport scheme (1), telehealth/community clinic closer to home (1). Could also mention sensory barriers if relevant to age. Discussion should interrelate the barriers and suggest how they could be overcome for Sonia specifically. Up to 6 marks.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the impact of personal obstacles on an individual's ability to follow recommendations to improve their health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks: Lower band (1-2): Limited identification of obstacles with little evaluation. Lower-mid band (3-4): Some obstacles identified with partial evaluation of their impact. Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear explanation of multiple obstacles (emotional, time, resources, targets, support) with developed evaluation of how they prevent individuals from improving health. Top band (7-8): Comprehensive evaluation covering range of obstacles, explaining how each one impacts the individual differently, considering how obstacles interact (e.g. lack of support makes emotional obstacles worse), and reaching a judgement on which obstacles are hardest to overcome and why. Considers how obstacles can be addressed through person-centred support.

practice_questions.text: Tariq is 50 and has been diagnosed with high blood pressure (155/100 mmHg). His GP has recommended that he reduces salt in his diet, starts exercising and attends a stress management course. Tariq works 60 hours a week in a restaurant, lives alone and has no family nearby. He also struggles with anxiety. Identify and explain the barriers and obstacles Tariq may face when following these recommendations. Suggest how each could be overcome.
practice_questions.marks: Lower band (1-3): Superficial identification with little reference to Tariq's situation. Lower-mid band (4-5): Some barriers/obstacles identified but not clearly distinguished or linked to Tariq. Upper-mid band (6-8): Clear distinction between barriers and obstacles. Barriers: geographical (stress management course location), financial (cost of gym), time (long working hours making appointments difficult). Obstacles: time constraints (60 hours/week), emotional/psychological (anxiety), lack of support (lives alone, no family nearby). Suggests ways to overcome e.g. telehealth for stress management, short exercise at home, community support group. Top band (9-10): Comprehensive response correctly categorising each difficulty as barrier or obstacle with justification. Person-centred suggestions for overcoming each one. Makes connections (e.g. anxiety obstacle worsened by lack of support obstacle). Suggests both formal and informal support.
